preamble: Deaspiration of the aspirated alveolar stop [tʰ] to plain [t]. In Ancient Greek it is conditioned by Grassmann's law: when two aspirates occur in successive syllables, the first loses its aspiration, so inherited *tʰ became t before a following aspirate (τίθημι, τριχός, τάφος, ταχύς).

examples.note: Grassmann's law: the reduplicating syllable loses aspiration before the aspirated root.
The root keeps its initial aspirate in the nominative θρίξ thríx, where the final aspirate is lost before s.
Compare θάπτειν tháptein 'to bury', where the second aspirate is lost before the t-suffix.
Compare the comparative θάσσων thássōn 'faster', which keeps the initial aspirate.

sources: Sihler, A. L. (1995). New Comparative Grammar of Greek and Latin. Oxford University Press. https://doi.org/10.1093/oso/9780195083453.001.0001
